extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal scholars, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and analyzes legal standards and doctrinal tests governing patentable subject matter (with emphasis on business-method patents), as articulated by courts and the PTO in cases like State Street, Alappat, Bilski, and related agency guidance. Useful for evaluating whether a claimed invention satisfies §101 and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO instruction on business-method claims (1996 Examination Guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be categorized as methods of doing business; instead, such claims should be treated like any other process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issued in February 1996 in the PTO’s "Examination Guideline for Computer-Related Inventions." The guideline recognizes that agency personnel "have had difficulty in properly treating claims directed to methods of doing business" and states the agency’s decision to treat business methods as ordinary process claims as a solution to maintaining a separate business-method category.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO White Paper view of "business method claim format"
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO described the 'business method claim format' as having been 'used in various forms throughout' the twentieth century and characterized the increase in its use as an 'inevitable end result' of technological progress; State Street merely 'triggered an awareness of the "business method claim" as a viable form of patent protection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Released July 2000. The White Paper presents the agency’s view that business-method claim formats are longstanding and legitimate claim forms and treats State Street as drawing attention to an existing practice rather than creating new law.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Useful, concrete, and tangible result" test (State Street / In re Alappat)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is patentable if it produces a 'useful, concrete and tangible result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous articulation in State Street (and earlier promulgated in In re Alappat). The article notes that this test was central to State Street’s analysis but that the Federal Circuit’s later en banc Bilski decision held that the 'useful, concrete and tangible result' analysis can no longer be considered good law (i.e., the test was repudiated by later Federal Circuit en banc authority). Justice Breyer in LabCorp commented that the Supreme Court has never endorsed such a literal statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is a patentable 'process' under §101 only if it is machine-implemented or involves the transformation of physical subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted by the PTO and crystallized by the PTO and accepted by an en banc Federal Circuit as the 'machine-or-transformation' test, which the PTO used to reject Bilski (characterizing his method as 'non-machine-implemented' and not involving transformation). The Supreme Court in Bilski rejected the machine-or-transformation test as the sole test for §101, holding that it cannot be the exclusive touchstone for determining whether a process is patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No categorical business-method exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'process' in §101 does not categorically exclude business methods; a business method can, in some circumstances, be eligible for patenting under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although State Street had explicitly rejected a business-method exception and the Federal Circuit largely reaffirmed that, the Supreme Court in Bilski held a majority that business methods are not categorically excluded from §101. At the same time, multiple Justices expressed unease about the wisdom/validity of some business-method patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court textualism and broad reading of §101 ('anything under the sun that is made by man')
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101's statutory language is 'extremely broad,' and courts should generally use ordinary, contemporary, common meaning in interpreting 'process' and other statutory terms; courts 'should not read into the patent laws limitations and conditions which the legislature has not expressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Supreme Court language from Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Diehr, and J.E.M. Ag Supply. The article argues the Court’s turn toward textualism was decisive in Bilski, driving reluctance to adopt restrictive per se rules excluding business methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of unpatentable subject matter: natural phenomena, principles of nature, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural phenomena and principles of nature are unpatentable; abstractions are also unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has recognized these limits on §101. The article notes that these categories do not map neatly onto business methods (many business methods may be concrete and specific rather than 'abstract'), so exclusion on these grounds must be applied carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and non-obviousness remain separate, critical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claimed process satisfies §101 subject-matter eligibility, it still must satisfy novelty (§102) and non-obviousness (§103) requirements; business-method applications may fail on these grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Bilski application, which had 'numerous problems' under basic patent doctrines—particularly that claimed hedging strategies had long been known and were likely not novel or were obvious. The PTO’s rejection of Bilski under §101 (machine-or-transformation) did not eliminate the relevance of §§102/103 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional/legislative response and Section 273 (special limitations for business-method patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacted Section 273, imposing special limitations of rights applicable to business-method patents, which has been construed as evidence that Congress addressed business-method issues and impacted the legal landscape for such patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner argued Congress 'had embraced' State Street by adding §273; the government and others referenced §273 in litigation to show legislative engagement with business-method patent issues. Section 273 thus functions as a policy/ statutory consideration distinct from §101 eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/claim-format considerations (business-method claim format as an established claim form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'business method claim format' has been used in various forms historically, and some business-method patents present detailed, specific, and well-defined procedures that resemble engineering solutions rather than abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples (e.g., a 2008 patent on valuing private equity investments) to show that some business-method patents are concrete and specific. This historical and technical context is relevant to assessing whether a claimed business method is an impermissible abstraction or a patentable application.
